svg.text: BY OPENING THIS BOOK YOU AGREE TO THE FOLLOWING. 1. Parties. This Agreement is between you (“the Reader,” “the Spouse,” or, in nine states, “half”) and a contract you have never seen, which has nonetheless been running your finances since approximately the first dance. 2. Subject matter. The Book describes the agreement you entered when you got married: who owns the paycheck, who owes the hospital, and who gets the

house, the dog, the 401(k), and the kidney (nobody; see Chapter 16). It is several thousand pages long. You signed the last page. There was cake. 3. Governing law. Wherever you happen to be living when it ends. You may change the terms at any time by moving to Texas. You will not be notified. 4. Amendments. The State may rewrite any term on a Tuesday afternoon without telling you. You may also rewrite some of them,

provided you hire two lawyers, disclose everything, and do not do it on the way to the airport. 5. Dispute resolution. One judge, no jury, a list of factors with no numbers attached, and the word “equitable,” which does not mean equal and does not mean anything else in particular either. 6. Representations. The Reader represents that their chance of divorce is zero. The Book acknowledges this and has some follow-up

questions. 7. Beneficiaries. Whoever you named on a form in 1998. 8. Warranties. None. This Book is not legal advice, was not written by a lawyer, and cannot tell you how your case will come out; neither, the Book respectfully submits, can your lawyer. 9. Remedies. Reading it. Preferably with the other party. 10. Term. Until death or a judge’s signature, whichever comes first. 11. Price. As marked. The Contract

itself was issued to you free of charge, which should have made you suspicious. 12. Severability. If any joke in this Book is found to be unenforceable, the remaining jokes shall continue in full force and effect. 13. Entire agreement. It isn’t. See inside. 14. Assignment. Your rights under this Agreement may be assigned to your former spouse by a form you completed on the first day of a job you no longer remember

having. 15. Notices. None will be sent. 16. Force majeure. Includes, without limitation, acts of God, acts of Congress, acts of the Florida legislature, and your mother-in-law. 17. Confidentiality. The terms of this Agreement are strictly confidential, in the sense that nobody has ever been able to find them. 18. Indemnification. You agree to pay your spouse’s hospital bill. You did not know that. You’re welcome.

19. Definitions. “Equitable” means as the judge sees fit. “Separate property” means property you have not yet deposited in the joint account. “Forever” is not a defined term. 20. Pets. The dog is a couch. See Chapter 18. The dog disagrees. 21. Survival. Clauses 7 and 18 survive the termination of this Agreement, your spouse, and you. 22. Counterparts. This Agreement was executed in one counterpart, which the county

kept. 23. Waiver. No waiver of any right in a retirement plan shall be effective unless signed after the wedding, on the plan’s own form, before a notary. Nobody told you that either. 24. Third-party beneficiaries. The Internal Revenue Service. 25. Interpretation. Headings are for convenience only. So, it turns out, were the vows. 26. Acknowledgment. By reading this far you have read more of this Agreement than you

ever read of your marriage contract. The author thanks you, and suggests that you now go and check the form in Clause 7. BY OPENING THIS BOOK YOU AGREE TO THE FOLLOWING. 1. Parties.
